title: Pre-teach only the words that block reading
statement: Pre-teach only words without which comprehension breaks down; support the rest in place, replace them or teach them after reading, and never introduce a word by asking what it means.
example: In one audited grade-5 lesson, one pinned blocking word was pre-taught, and two other words given the same full cycle were ruled a violation.
detail: A reading quality canon applied in a grade-5 audit pre-teaches only the words needed to prevent comprehension breakdown and teaches the rest after reading, and its word-audit rule assigns every likely blocker to pre-teaching, inline support, replacement or review, with meanings that are not circular. In the audited lesson the pinned blocking word was pre-taught before the first read with pronunciation support and a say-back, which conformed, while two other words, one of them a K-3 science word, got the same full cycle and were ruled a violation.
against: The record teach-a-word-before-using-it holds that no word students may not know is used before the lesson teaches it, and a curriculum thread map it cites wants each unit's technical terms taught before reading, so the two disagree on words students first meet in the passage. The open record words-taught-before-reading holds a rule for opening films that calls the film the best place to teach a word, which would teach words before the reading whether or not they block understanding.

evidence.quote: Only the words needed to prevent comprehension breakdown are pre-taught; the rest are taught after reading.
A word audit assigns every likely blocker to preteach, inline support, replacement, or review; meanings are non-circular; pronunciation and active use work in the rendered context.
`decomposer` pre-taught before first read with syllable pronunciation support and say-back.
`producer` and `habitat` receive the full blocking-word-style deep-teach cycle, though habitat is a K-3 science word and neither is the pinned blocking word.
Only the words needed to prevent comprehension breakdown are pre-taught; the rest are taught after reading
An unfamiliar word is never introduced with a guess-opener ("who can tell me what X means?")
Distinguish light in-text glossing ('pause and punch', keep reading) from the few words taught to production after the read — not uniform deep treatment for every taught word
